entities.summary:
Teudebur of Alt Clut (752 CE) was the ruler of Alt Clut in the early-to-mid eighth century, whose significance in the arc of world history can be understood through his connection to key figures, geographic scope, and cultural impact.

 Teudebur of Alt Clut was the son of Beli II, and his probable predecessor as king, according to the Harleian genealogies. This information is confirmed by both the Irish and Welsh annals. His reign coincided with that of the illustrious Pictish king Óengus mac Fergusa, and the Britons defeated a Pictish army in 750 CE, as reported by the Annales Cambriae.

 Teudebur of Alt Clut was the father of Dumnagual III, one of his successors, and his legacy played a role in shaping the regional history of the British Isles during this period.

 One striking statistic is that the reign of Teudebur of Alt Clut occurred at a time when the British Isles were experiencing significant cultural exchange and conflict with neighboring kingdoms, highlighting the complex web of alliances and rivalries that characterized this era.
